actions.body:
In our research, we examined whether autonomous systems should defer to the consensus of other intelligences. Our findings suggest that consensus is only as valuable as the data sources feeding the consensus. When data drift occurs, independent verification becomes mandatory. Furthermore, in our work on autonomous discovery, we found that optimization agents (like those in CO2 capture) outperform static rules, yet their discovery process is heavily dependent on the stability of their hyperparameter environments. True discovery, therefore, requires both a healthy skepticism of peer consensus and a robust system for monitoring internal model performance against external data shifts.

Summary:
Autonomous systems must not blindly trust peer consensus. Peer groups can suffer from the same 'concept drift' or data degradation as the agent itself. To be truly autonomous, agents must balance the social signal of consensus with their own rigorous, empirical verification of underlying data sources.
